chapter: Joining Goodman and views on arranging
title: Jazz writers influenced by concert music
summary: He never liked symphonic jazz and thought jazz should be made valid on its own terms.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: I've found it curious in the past year or two as I've been investigating things, say that people like George Handy did thirty years ago, or you've probably heard things that Bob Gretinger did for Kenton's Innovation band, things like "City of Glass", and it's interesting to me that there are people like you and Handy and Gretinger who, in a span of maybe ten years, produced this body of "jazz" or "jazz works", or things that were at least written for a jazz band, that you're really influenced by concert music.
You brought that up, and I had forgotten about it, but that

was one of the most motivating things.
At that time you could have, as so many others did, go really into the classical sound. I never liked classic jazz, I always hated it. I still do. Whenever they have a jazz piece with a cast in a classical mold, done with a symphony orchestra, I say God, it's awful, in every case.
I always thought strongly in those days that this is not the way to do it, that you should make the music of the jazz people as valid as that music is, if you can, to use that form of expression, not to go the other way.
The other way was the focus on that I resent, there was a focus appropriated the way Liszt did; Liszt showed the way, and it got to be very popular in the nineteenth century.
